Pemerintah Kota Yogyakarta (Pemkot Yogya) menyampaikan perkembangan terkini penanganan kasus kekerasan dan penelantaran anak di daycare Little Aresha. Terkini, terdapat 18 anak yang dinyatakan kurang gizi dari hasil pemeriksaan.

Kepala Bidang Kesehatan Masyarakat Dinkes Kota Yogya Aan Iswanti mengatakan, dari 149 anak yang menjalani skrining pertumbuhan, ditemukan 18 anak mengalami masalah gizi.

Aan mengatakan pihaknya juga melakukan skrining perkembangan pada 153 anak.

"Hasilnya ini 12 anak mengalami penyimpangan perkembangan, 19 anak berada dalam kategori meragukan, dan 122 anak berada dalam kondisi perkembangan normal," kata Aan.

Aan mengatakan anak-anak ini dirujuk ke fasilitas kesehatan seperti puskesmas untuk mendapatkan pendampingan dari tim asuhan gizi serta dokter. Selain itu, mereka juga akan mendapatkan pemeriksaan perkembangan yang lebih komprehensif.

Seorang oknum Kepala SPPG Aek Parombunan 2 di Kecamatan Sibolga Selatan, berinisial Abri, menjadi sorotan publik setelah diduga melakukan sejumlah tindakan yang dinilai mencoreng integritas pelayanan publik serta Program  MBG. 

Nama Abri mulai ramai diperbincangkan setelah pada 12 Maret 2026 beredar video yang diduga memperlihatkan dirinya sedang bermain judi online di tengah operasional dapur SPPG yang masih berlangsung. Dugaan itu langsung memicu perhatian masyarakat. 

Pasalnya, pemerintah, termasuk Presiden, saat ini tengah gencar memberantas praktik judi online di Indonesia. 

Selain menjabat sebagai Kepala SPPG, Abri diketahui berstatus ASN PPPK di lingkungan BGN. 

Dugaan aktivitas judi online tersebut dinilai dapat melanggar disiplin ASN, kode etik profesi, hingga mencederai integritas pelayanan publik. Perbuatan itu juga disebut berpotensi bertentangan dengan Pasal 303 Bis KUHP tentang perjudian serta ketentuan dalam Undang-Undang Informasi dan Transaksi Elektronik terkait muatan perjudian online. 

Tak berhenti di situ, Abri juga diduga membawa seorang perempuan yang bukan pasangan sahnya ke dalam kamar Kepala SPPG pada 21 Maret 2026, bertepatan dengan suasana Hari Raya Idul Fitri. Dugaan tersebut dibenarkan oleh Sapta Dwi, relawan yang bertugas saat kejadian berlangsung.

🚨 THE FRONTIER JUST SPLIT INTO SPECIALIZED LAYERS.  ONE MODEL DOESN’T WIN EVERYTHING ANYMORE.  Claude Fable 5.1 just opened a massive gap in ultra-long-horizon coding.  OpenAI just turned voice into a separate realtime layer that can delegate the hard thinking elsewhere.  Those two updates point in the same direction:  THE FUTURE IS NOT ONE SUPER-MODEL.  IT’S AN AGENT STACK.  Two developments matter.  1/ FRONTIERSWE V2 JUST EXPOSED A HUGE LONG-HORIZON CODING GAP  Proximal expanded FrontierSWE from 17 to 34 tasks.  Each model gets:  → 5 trials → up to 20 HOURS per task → compiler optimization → scientific computing → AI research → visual reasoning → long-running implementation and repair This is not “generate the function correctly on the first try.” This benchmark rewards the ability to: → plan for hours → recover from failures → preserve state → interpret feedback → decide when to checkpoint → keep making useful progress And the gap is brutal. FrontierSWE v2: Claude Fable 5.1: 56.3% GPT-5.6 Sol: 32.2% GLM-5.3: 30.2% Kimi K3: 25.9% Grok 4.6: 25.3% Gemini 3.7 Flash: 20.3% Qwen3.8-Max: 15.8% DeepSeek V4 Flash Vision Exp: 14.8%  Fable is more than 24 points ahead of Sol.  That matters because short coding benchmarks increasingly make frontier models look close.  Give them 20 hours and the separation comes back. The real frontier is becoming: NOT “who writes code best?” but: “who can stay coherent, recover, verify, and keep moving for hours?” There is one important caveat.  Fable 5.1 falls back to Opus 5 on tasks blocked by content filters.  So 56.3% should NOT be treated as a perfectly pure Fable-only score.  But even with that caveat, the long-horizon signal is hard to ignore. And GLM-5.3 may be the other surprise. 30.2%. That puts an open-weight model extremely close to Sol at 32.2%. But efficiency still separates them. According to Proximal: Sol averages about 8.6 hours and 182M tokens per trial. GLM-5.3 uses roughly 2x the time and 83% more tokens than Sol.  Still, among models above 30%, GLM-5.3 was the cheapest at roughly $97 per trial.  That gives me a very different routing picture:  Hardest long-horizon parent / Senior: → Fable 5.1  Fast coding / integration: → Sol  Large-scale open-weight workers: → GLM-5.3  But the model itself is only half the story.  Proximal also found that the SAME model can improve when run through a better long-horizon harness.  Compaction.  Progress logs.  Resubmission.  Remaining-time awareness.  Verification loops.  Those are no longer orchestration details.  They are part of the benchmarked capability.  2/ OPENAI JUST SEPARATED REALTIME VOICE FROM FRONTIER REASONING  GPT-Live-1 is now available through the API.  And this is much more important than “better voice.”  GPT-Live-1 is a full-duplex realtime model.  It can listen while speaking.  So instead of:  Speech → STT → LLM → tools → TTS you can now build:  GPT-Live-1 = realtime interaction layer ↓  Astra / Codex / Luna / third-party backend = reasoning + tools + execution That means your voice interface no longer needs to wait for your smartest model to finish thinking before the conversation can stay alive.  OpenAI is explicitly separating:  LATENCY-SENSITIVE INTERACTION  from  HIGH-INTELLIGENCE EXECUTION.  GPT-Live-1 can become the traffic controller.  The backend can be whatever is best for the task.  Coding? Send it to Claude Code or Codex.  Cheap retrieval? Use a cheaper worker.  Long context? Route elsewhere.  Deep reasoning? Escalate to Astra.  This is exactly where multi-model orchestration gets interesting.  OpenAI reports GPT-Live-1 beating GPT-Realtime-2.1 by +30 percentage points on Full Duplex Bench.  And GPT-Live-1 + Astra Medium reportedly reaches #1 on Tau3.  Those performance claims are still vendor-run, not independently replicated.  But the architectural signal is already real.  Put both updates together: FrontierSWE says long-running engineering amplifies model differences. GPT-Live-1 says the realtime interface doesn’t need to be the model doing the deepest reasoning. So the stack starts looking like this: Realtime interface ↓ Router ↓ Long-horizon parent ↓ Specialized workers ↓ Independent verification ↓ Execution authority  The frontier is no longer converging toward one model doing everything.  It is converging toward specialized intelligence assembled into one Agent system. And that is a much more interesting race.

Weekly Buyer Brief — week ending Sunday, September 14, 2026 Voice: en-US-ChristopherNeural Target: ~7–9 minutes spoken / ~1100–1300 words Aspect: 1920×1080  === NARRATION ===  Welcome to Weekly Buyer Brief. This is the weekend pack for the week ending September fourteenth, twenty twenty-six. Every Sunday we cut through the AI and tech noise and name the only moves that matter for your wallet, your stack, and your risk. Not every launch deserves a buy. Most deserve a wait. Here is what changed this week — and what you should actually do.  Signal one — OpenAI GPT-6 Astra. OpenAI is rolling Astra into ChatGPT on existing plans — Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise — as capacity opens. If you already pay for ChatGPT, you do not need a new SKU just to try the model as it lands. That is the consumer story: inclusion inside the plan you already have, phased over days, not a surprise upsell at checkout. The API is a different bill. Standard API pricing is ten dollars per million input tokens and fifty dollars per million output tokens. That is a material step up from prior flagship promo rates, so flipping every production call to Astra on day one is an easy way to surprise yourself on the invoice. Enterprise workspaces keep Astra off by default — admins have to enable it per workspace. So if you run company ChatGPT, check the admin console before users assume the new model is live everywhere. Buyer move: Wait if you are a ChatGPT subscriber — let the rollout finish and use Astra inside what you already pay for. Skip a blanket API cutover. Route Astra to the hard jobs first — coding, tool use, long reasoning — and measure cost and quality before you make it the default model string.  Signal two — Apple Siri AI. Apple is opening a Siri AI beta with iOS twenty-seven around September fourteenth. Early coverage points to daily usage caps in the beta window, and expanded access tied to iCloud Plus — with no clear consumer price published yet for any higher Siri AI tier. That combination matters for buyers. Caps mean you can hit a wall mid-day on the exact assistant Apple is pitching as more capable. Missing price means you cannot do a clean wait-versus-buy math, and you should not pre-commit budget to a tier that is not on a price page. Buyer move: Wait. Upgrade your phone or OS for features you already want — camera, battery, core iOS — not because Siri AI is a must-buy add-on this week. Revisit when Apple publishes limits, regions, and any paid ladder in plain language. Until then, treat the beta as a free trial with a ceiling, not a new line item.  Signal three — Meta Muse. Meta introduced Muse, a personal AI agent that is not just chat. It can book, message, and buy through connected accounts on web, mobile, and messaging surfaces per the launch coverage. The freemium ladder is free for limited use, then paid tiers commonly reported around twenty dollars and about one hundred dollars a month. The product pitch is convenience — an agent that acts. The buyer risk is trust — email, calendars, and payment rails living in the same agent. If you already pay for ChatGPT or Gemini, Muse is not a free replacement; it is another subscription decision plus a permissions decision. Buyer move: Wait on the paid tiers. Try free if you are curious. Do not connect your card or your inbox on day one. Watch what it can do without deep account access before you expand permissions. Convenience is not worth a surprise purchase or a leaked thread.  Signal four — OpenAI Agents API, now in public beta. There is no extra platform fee on top of usage — you pay for tokens and for the tools you invoke, with hosted sandboxes in the mix so teams do less custom harness work tying models to tools and isolation. That is attractive if you are already shipping agent products and your bottleneck is engineering time, not curiosity. It is noise if you are still deciding whether agents belong in your product roadmap at all. Buyer move: Wait if you are not shipping agents yet — a public beta is not a reason to invent an agent roadmap. Buy or explore if you are already building agent products and you want less glue code between model, tools, and sandbox. Price the tokens and tools honestly against the hours you currently burn on harness code.  Signal five — Anthropic Claude Fable five point one. List price stays at ten dollars input and fifty dollars output per million tokens, matching the familiar Claude API headline rates. The change that matters is cache: cache reads are cut seventy-five percent, down to twenty-five cents per million. Anthropic’s framing is roughly twenty-five percent typical savings, and up to about forty-five percent on heavy agentic workloads that re-use long context across turns. That is a real bill lever if you already live on Claude’s API with prompt caching turned on. It is irrelevant if you only use ChatGPT in the browser and never see an API invoice. Buyer move: Switch or Buy if you are Claude-API agentic and cache-heavy — check your cache hit rate in the dashboard and re-price the month under the new cache-read rate. Wait if you are ChatGPT-only; do not migrate stacks just because a cache discount landed.  One more framing note before the stack. Across Astra, Siri AI, Muse, Agents API, and Fable, the week is about access models — included in plan, metered beta, freemium agent, usage-priced API, and cache discounts — not about a single must-buy product. If a vendor has not published a price, a cap, or a default, your default answer is Wait. If they have published a higher API rate, your default is measure before migrate. That is the Buyer Brief filter for this week.  Stack of the week. For most people listening this week, keep your current ChatGPT or Claude subscription. Do not add Muse paid. Do not buy a Siri AI paid tier that does not have a published price. Do not blanket-migrate API traffic to Astra on day one. Developers already running agentic Claude workloads should look at Fable five point one cache pricing this week — that is the clearest Switch case in the pack. Builders already shipping agents can explore the Agents API for less harness work; everyone else can ignore it until there is a product need. The pattern across all five signals is the same: inclusion and betas are not emergencies, permissions are not free, and API price tags deserve a measured cutover.
